concepts.def: Shaping musical lines like sentences with breath and shape.
How notes are attacked and released (staccato, legato).
Volume levels from very quiet (pp) to very loud (ff).
Slight expressive flexing of tempo for musical effect.
Adjusting volume so each part is heard clearly in an ensemble.
Matching tone and timbre with other ensemble players.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A musical phrase is like a sentence — it has a start, a peak and an ending. Most phrases naturally grow toward a high note then taper down.

Try a small crescendo rising to the peak and a decrescendo falling away. Breathe (or lift) between phrases so the music feels alive rather than mechanical.

Legato notes are smooth and connected — think singing. Staccato notes are short and detached, shown with a dot above the note. Marcato notes are stressed and emphatic.

Composers often mark these clearly, but you can also choose articulation to bring contrast between sections.

Great ensembles listen as much as they play. Match your blend by copying the tone of your section, and adjust balance so the melody is always heard above accompaniment.

Watch the leader's breath, bowing or count-in. If someone drifts, gently come back to the group pulse rather than racing.
